title: Time-Domain NIRS Detection of Neurovascular Coupling Impairment: A Potential Biomarker of Psychological Stress
content: Chronic psychological stress is associated with adverse health outcomes and substantial socioeconomic burden. Early identification of psychological stress is important for public health, but no biomarker specific to psychological stress has yet been established. Growing evidence suggests that neurovascular coupling (NVC) is impaired under stress conditions. To test this hypothesis, we investigated the relationship between NVC responses and baseline anxiety in 35 healthy participants. Cerebrovascular responses during a finger-tapping task were measured using time-domain near-infrared spectroscopy (TD-NIRS). Baseline anxiety was assessed using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) as an indicator related to psychological stress. After adjusting for age, resting total hemoglobin, and the integration time used for TD-NIRS measurements, the difference in NVC responses between participants with higher and lower STAI-State scores did not reach statistical significance when all participants were included (P = 0.050). After excluding two outliers identified using a 1.0 × IQR criterion, the difference in NVC responses between the two groups became statistically significant (P = 0.027). Participants with higher STAI-State scores showed lower NVC responses than those with lower scores. These findings suggest that impaired NVC may serve as a physiological indicator of psychological stress.
